summary:
We developed the SPHEREx Time-Domain Sky Explorer & Planet X Hunter, an astronomical workstation engineered to uncover Planet Nine, cold brown dwarfs, and moving celestial objects.

The platform uses a 100% serverless, zero-install architecture that runs entirely client-side in any web browser with zero backend infrastructure or setup. It delivers high-performance analysis tools directly in-memory, including real-time difference imaging to reveal moving object dipoles, a 60 FPS blink comparator, rapid 102-band infrared scrubbing, and custom thermal filter grouping. It also integrates lockstep synchronized cross-checking with the CDS Aladin sky atlas (WISE, 2MASS, Gaia DR3) and one-click candidate dossier exports.

This project is important because searching the outer Solar System usually demands heavy compute clusters and specialized software. By removing server costs and installation friction, our tool democratizes space exploration—allowing anyone worldwide to hunt for planets in real-time survey data directly from their browser.
details:
The SPHEREx Sky Tracker is a browser-native, zero-backend public observatory tool designed for NASA's SPHEREx mission. By surveying the entire sky every ~6 months across 102 near-infrared bands (0.75–5.0 µm) with a 6.15″/pixel detector, SPHEREx collects multi-epoch datasets of over a billion sources. Our tool solves the core discovery challenge: answering instantly and visually, "Has SPHEREx observed this spot, when did it look, and how far did candidate objects move between those looks?"

Users simply enter an astronomical object name (e.g., WISE 0855−0714, Barnard’s Star, Comet 3I/ATLAS) or custom celestial coordinates (RA/Dec in decimal or sexagesimal). The client executes real-time queries directly in the browser to NASA/IPAC IRSA, CDS Sesame/SIMBAD, ESA Gaia DR3, and JPL Horizons. It projects a calibrated 2D gnomonic tangent-plane sky chart (North up, East left) plotting:

  1. Multi-epoch SPHEREx observation pointings color-coded chronologically along a single-hue sequential gradient.
  2. Target motion tracks computed via rigorous proper motion propagation (with cos δ correction) or orbital ephemerides, connected by vector lines with dated dots.
  3. Stationary Gaia background stars providing immediate visual contrast against movers.
  4. A calibrated 30″ scale bar and a 6.15″ SPHEREx detector pixel circle so citizens intuitively grasp the physical displacement in detector pixels. An interactive timeline scrubber animates the object across real survey passes, paired with live readouts ("Elapsed: X.XX yr · Target shifted Y.Y″ · Z.Z SPHEREx pixels") and a chronological observation table with direct links to IRSA data products.
